title: Laennec's stethoscope

confidence.note: Laennec dated the paper-tube episode to 1816 in his own treatise, published in 1819 and translated into English in 1821. What is softer is the popular emphasis on his shyness: his own account gives the patient's weight as the first reason the usual methods failed.

people: René-Théophile-Hyacinthe Laennec (1781–1826), physician at the Necker Hospital
Leopold Auenbrugger, Viennese physician who described chest percussion in 1761
Jean-Nicolas Corvisart, Laennec's teacher, who revived percussion in France
John Forbes, English physician who translated Laennec's treatise in 1821
summary: A rolled-up quire of paper let a Paris doctor hear a living heart, and turned the body's hidden sounds into evidence of disease.
body: In 1816 René Laennec, a physician at the Necker Hospital in Paris, was consulted by a young woman with the symptoms of heart disease. Tapping her chest and feeling it with his hand told him little, he later wrote, because of “the great degree of fatness,” and putting his ear to her chest was ruled out by her age and sex. He remembered that sound carries well through solid bodies, as when the scratch of a pin at one end of a piece of wood is heard at the other. So he rolled a quire of paper into a cylinder, set one end over her heart and the other at his ear, and heard the heart more clearly than he ever had with his bare ear.

Laennec worked in the Paris hospitals where doctors were learning to match what they found at the bedside with what they found at autopsy. One bedside technique already existed. In 1761 the Viennese physician Leopold Auenbrugger had published *Inventum novum*, on judging the state of the chest from the sound it made when tapped. The method was largely ignored until Laennec's teacher Jean-Nicolas Corvisart translated it into French and took it up.

Over the next three years Laennec listened to patients and checked what he heard against what dissection showed after death. He replaced the paper with a bored wooden cylinder that came apart for carrying and named it the stethoscope. His *De l'Auscultation médiate* of 1819 coined terms still in use, such as pectoriloquy and egophony, and taught doctors to tell apart diseases such as bronchiectasis, emphysema and pneumothorax in the living patient.

The two-volume book caused little stir at first, but John Forbes's English translation appeared in 1821 and the instrument spread. The real change was that diagnosis moved inside the body: a physician could now infer a damaged lung or valve before death rather than relying on the patient's account of symptoms. Laennec himself died of tuberculosis, the disease he had studied most closely, in August 1826, aged 45.

myth.tradition: Laennec invented the stethoscope because he was too shy or too proper to press his ear to a young woman's chest.
myth.record: Propriety was one reason, but his own account says percussion and touch failed because of the patient's weight, and that he had long listened with his bare ear in difficult cases. He presented the tube as a better way of hearing, not just a more modest one.

links.note: Paris hospital medicine paired bedside signs with autopsy findings.
The idea that disease sits in particular organs gave the sounds something to point to.
Eighty years later, another way to examine the inside of a living body.

title: Beaumont and the window in a stomach

confidence.note: Beaumont's 1833 book gives the dates of the wound and the experiments, and Osler examined the signed contracts and family correspondence. Whether St. Martin, poor and unable to write, could freely consent is a modern ethical judgment rather than a factual dispute.

place: Fort Mackinac, Michigan Territory, and later Plattsburgh and Washington
people: William Beaumont, U.S. Army surgeon
Alexis St. Martin (died 1880), French-Canadian voyageur whose wound left an opening into his stomach
summary: A gunshot left a young voyageur with a hole into his stomach, and an army surgeon spent years watching digestion through it.
body: On 6 June 1822 a musket fired from about a yard away tore open the side of Alexis St. Martin, an eighteen-year-old French-Canadian voyageur at Fort Mackinac. The army surgeon William Beaumont saved him, but the wound healed around an opening into the stomach. From 1825 Beaumont lowered food on silk strings through it and drew out gastric juice, showing that digestion was chemical as well as mechanical; his book appeared in 1833. St. Martin, who signed with a mark, was bound by contract as Beaumont's servant and subject. When he died in 1880, his family let the body decay before burying it eight feet deep, to keep doctors away.

links.note: A later and far graver case of research on a dependent subject.

title: Body-snatchers and the Anatomy Act

confidence.note: The Act, the Burke trial and the London murders are documented in court and parliamentary records. Modern sources date the earlier Murder Act to 1751 or 1752, and Burke and Hare's toll of at least 16 is the usual figure.

people: William Burke (executed 1829), murderer
William Hare, his accomplice, who testified against him
Robert Knox, Edinburgh anatomy lecturer who bought the bodies
summary: Murders committed to supply anatomy classes pushed Parliament to hand anatomists a new source of bodies: the poor who died in workhouses.
body: British anatomy schools in the 1820s needed far more corpses than the law supplied, since only executed murderers could legally be dissected, so grave-robbers filled the gap. In Edinburgh in 1828 William Burke and William Hare went further, killing at least 16 people and selling the bodies to the anatomist Robert Knox. Hare turned against Burke, who was hanged in 1829 and publicly dissected. After copycat killings in London in 1831, Parliament passed the Anatomy Act of 1832. It ended dissection as a punishment and gave licensed schools the unclaimed bodies of people who died in workhouses and hospitals, making dissection the fate of the poor.

links.note: Eighteenth-century anatomy teaching depended on the same illicit trade in bodies.

title: Cell theory

confidence.note: Schleiden's paper (1838) and Schwann's book (1839) are dated publications. Historians agree that their account of how cells form was wrong and was replaced by cell division in the 1850s; how to divide credit between Remak and Virchow for that correction is a matter of emphasis.

people: Matthias Schleiden, botanist
Theodor Schwann, physiologist in Johannes Müller's Berlin laboratory
Robert Remak (1815–1865), embryologist
Rudolf Virchow (1821–1902), pathologist
summary: Plants and animals turned out to be built from the same units, though the men who said so misunderstood where new cells came from.
body: In 1838 the botanist Matthias Schleiden argued that plant tissue was made of cells that formed around a nucleus, and he described his findings to Theodor Schwann before publishing them. Schwann, working in Johannes Müller's Berlin laboratory, found the same structures in animal tissues. In his *Microscopic Investigations* of 1839 he concluded that one principle of development, the cell, held for all living things.

They were wrong, though, about where cells came from. Schwann thought new cells condensed out of a structureless fluid he called the cytoblastema, a reasonable reading of the microscopes of the day and close to Müller's own teaching about a formative fluid. In the early 1850s Robert Remak and Rudolf Virchow, both Müller's students, replaced this with cell division. Remak supplied much of the evidence, but it was Virchow's slogan *omnis cellula e cellula*, every cell from a cell, that settled the matter and became the basis of his cellular pathology.

myth.tradition: Schleiden and Schwann established that all cells come from pre-existing cells.
myth.record: They believed new cells crystallized out of a fluid. Division as the source of all cells came from Remak's and Virchow's work in the 1850s.

links.note: Cells had been seen and named since the 1660s.
Virchow carried the cell into pathology.

title: Chadwick's sanitary report

confidence.note: The report (July 1842) and the Public Health Act (1848) are dated documents. That sanitary engineering cut deaths in the long run is accepted, but historians stress its mixed early effects and the political choices behind Chadwick's framing.

people: Edwin Chadwick (1800–1890), lawyer and Poor Law administrator
summary: A Poor Law official blamed filth and foul air for the diseases of the poor, and his wrong theory still produced sewers and clean water.
body: In July 1842 Edwin Chadwick, a lawyer who had helped design the harsh New Poor Law of 1834, published his *Report on the Sanitary Condition of the Labouring Population of Great Britain*. Drawing on local reports from across the country, it blamed epidemic disease on “atmospheric impurities produced by decomposing animal and vegetable substances,” damp, filth and overcrowding, and claimed that filth killed more people each year than any modern war. Good wages, it argued, gave no protection.

Chadwick's interest was partly financial: sick breadwinners pushed families onto poor relief. His answer was engineering rather than higher wages: drainage, sewers and abundant piped water. The Public Health Act of 1848 let local boards tax property owners to pay for them.

The theory was wrong. Cholera and typhoid spread through contaminated water, not foul air. Removing waste and supplying clean water still cut those routes, but not at once. Early sewers often emptied into rivers that also supplied drinking water, and in some towns they made pollution worse.

links.note: Snow showed in 1854 that cholera travelled in water, not air.
An earlier state that built sewers and aqueducts.
Another sanitary reformer who believed in miasma.

title: Women enter the profession

confidence.note: Blackwell's 1849 degree, Crumpler's 1864 degree and the British milestones are well documented. The story of the Geneva students voting her in as a joke comes from later accounts but is consistently reported; Erxleben's 1754 doctorate is documented here only in secondary sources.

people: Elizabeth Blackwell (1821–1910), first woman to earn an M.D. from an American medical school
Rebecca Lee Crumpler (1831–1895?), first African American woman to earn an M.D.
James Barry, born Margaret Bulkley, army surgeon who graduated from Edinburgh in 1812
Elizabeth Garrett Anderson (1836–1917), first woman to qualify as a doctor in the United Kingdom

summary: Elizabeth Blackwell's 1849 degree came after rejections, a students' joke and a long line of women who had found other ways in.
body: In 1849 Elizabeth Blackwell graduated from Geneva Medical College in upstate New York, the first woman to earn an M.D. from an American medical school. Every school in New York and Philadelphia, and twelve more in the Northeast, had turned her down. Geneva's faculty, sure the all-male students would refuse, let them vote on her admission. They voted yes, reportedly as a joke.

She was not the first woman to practise medicine with a degree. Dorothea Erxleben took a doctorate at Halle in 1754 with the favor of Frederick the Great, and Margaret Bulkley graduated from Edinburgh in 1812 as James Barry, living as a man through a long army career. In 1864 Rebecca Lee Crumpler, a nurse for eight years, became the first African American woman to earn an M.D.

Britain moved slowly. Elizabeth Garrett qualified in 1865 through the examinations of the Society of Apothecaries. Sophia Jex-Blake and the other “Edinburgh Seven” enrolled at Edinburgh in 1869 but were later shut out, and only the Medical Act of 1876 opened qualifying examinations to women.

myth.tradition: Elizabeth Blackwell was the first woman doctor.
myth.record: She was the first woman to earn an M.D. from an American medical school. Women had long worked as healers and midwives, Dorothea Erxleben took a German medical doctorate in 1754, and James Barry graduated from Edinburgh in 1812.

title: The hypodermic syringe

confidence.note: Wood's own 1855 paper describes his first injection in November 1853, and Pravaz's syringe is of the same year. Credit was disputed at the time, notably with Charles Hunter, and Rynd's 1844 hollow needle came earlier.

people: Alexander Wood, Edinburgh physician
Charles-Gabriel Pravaz, French physician
Francis Rynd (1801–1861), Irish physician
Charles Hunter, London surgeon who named the method hypodermic
summary: A small syringe built to treat birthmarks and aneurysms became the way to put morphine straight into the body.
body: In 1844 the Irish physician Francis Rynd used a hollow needle to relieve a patient's facial pain. In 1853 Charles-Gabriel Pravaz in France built a piston syringe to inject coagulant into aneurysms. That November in Edinburgh, Alexander Wood used a small syringe made in London for treating birthmarks to inject morphine beside the painful nerve of an elderly woman with neuralgia, and she slept through the night. Wood believed the drug acted locally. The London surgeon Charles Hunter showed it worked wherever it was injected. By 1870 Clifford Allbutt was warning about patients injecting themselves every day.

myth.tradition: Wood's first injection was given to his own dying wife, who became the first person addicted to injected morphine.
myth.record: Wood's published account describes his first patient as an elderly unmarried woman with neuralgia. The story about his wife is repeated in modern reviews but does not appear in his own report.

links.note: Morphine had been isolated half a century earlier.
Doctors' fears about opioid dependence began with the syringe.
